title: SYSK Selects: How Disco Works
summary: SYSK Selects rerun of the episode "How Disco Works," first released July 2012, chosen by Josh as a favorite. The hosts trace disco from its roots in New York's underground DJ-driven parties (David Mancuso's the Loft), gay clubs, and Philadelphia soul, through the coining of the term "disco" by Vince Aletti, to its mainstream peak and the backlash, including the Disco Demolition Night at Comiskey Park in 1979. They discuss disco's class, racial, and gay cultural dimensions, its fashion, Saturday Night Fever, its influence on hip hop and modern electronic dance music, and the deaths of Donna Summer and Robin Gibb. The episode closes with Chuck's presentation about his trip to Max Fun Con, with plugs for Jesse Thorn, Riff Tracks, My Brother My Brother and Me, David Rees, and others.
topics: Peter Shapiro Turn the Beat Around

segments.title: Rerun intro and Josh's pick
segments.summary: Josh introduces this SYSK Selects episode, explaining he chose How Disco Works, first released July 2012. The hosts banter about the Hustle dance.

segments.title: Disco Demolition Night
segments.summary: The hosts describe the July 12, 1979 Disco Demolition Night at Comiskey Park between the White Sox and Tigers, promoted by Chicago rock DJ Steve Dahl after he was fired when his station switched to disco. Around 90,000 people attended, a crowd broke through the gates, records were blown up, the field was trashed, and the second game was forfeited. They discuss the anti-disco sentiment and 'disco sucks' culture.

segments.title: Disco origins in New York parties and gay clubs
segments.summary: The hosts trace disco's origins to David Mancuso's invitation-only loft parties starting around 1970, the DJ-driven format, Terry Noel and clubs like Arthur, and gay clubs playing Philadelphia soul. Examples discussed include Barry White and Jerry Butler.

segments.title: Naming disco and the discotheque
segments.summary: The hosts discuss Manu Dibango's 1972 track Soul Makossa as an early disco song, and Vince Aletti's 1973 Rolling Stone piece that first described the music as disco. They explain that disco is short for discotheque, a club with recorded music rather than a live band, which challenged rock-era live performance and album sales.

segments.title: Disco hits, Philly producers, and music quality
segments.summary: The hosts list disco hits and artists such as Chic, Gloria Gaynor, Casey and the Sunshine Band, and Village People, and discuss Gamble and Huff, Philadelphia International, and Giorgio Moroder. They argue disco is musically difficult and that the strongest criticism is lyrical.

segments.title: Disco's class, race, and gay culture politics
segments.summary: The hosts discuss how disco began as music of working-class, Latino, Italian, Black, and gay communities in the Bronx and Queens, was taken up by the elite at Studio 54, and was opposed by a rock establishment that the hosts argue was partly motivated by racism and homophobia. They note disco's escapist nature and lyrics criticized as apolitical.

segments.title: Saturday Night Fever, fashion, and disco venues
segments.summary: The hosts discuss Saturday Night Fever and the Nik Cohn article it was based on, which Cohn later said he fabricated. They cover disco fashion including polyester, spandex, and the white suit, and mention former disco venues in New York that now house other businesses.

segments.title: Record industry, decline, legacy, and influence on hip hop
segments.summary: The hosts argue the record industry's decision to stop producing disco records, along with the Disco Demolition Night symbolism, drove disco's decline, and that disco's four-on-the-floor beat lives on in later pop and electronic music. They cover disco's influence on hip hop, citing Sugarhill Gang's Rapper's Delight built on Chic's Good Times, and current acts like Scissor Sisters and Hercules and Love Affair. They also remember Donna Summer and Robin Gibb, who died recently.
topics: Peter Shapiro Turn the Beat Around

segments.title: Chuck's Max Fun Con presentation and sign-off
segments.summary: Chuck presents on his Max Fun Con trip, plugging Jesse Thorn, Riff Tracks, My Brother My Brother and Me, David Rees's artisanal pencil sharpening, Roman Mars's Invisible, and comedians such as Cameron Esposito and John Hodgman. The episode closes with a song and contact information.
